body_md: `dyn Trait` is **dynamic dispatch** (vtable, one size); `impl Trait` is static (monomorphized). Use dyn for heterogeneous lists `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>`, impl for speed.
hook: Same keyword, opposite tradeoffs — dyn vs impl decides speed vs flexibility.
output: // compiles: render_all dispatches each draw() via vtable

quiz.explain: dyn Trait dispatches through a vtable at runtime, allowing mixed types; impl Trait is resolved at compile time and monomorphized.
options: They are aliases; both compile the same way
impl uses a vtable; dyn is monomorphized
dyn uses a vtable; impl is monomorphized
Both use vtables, but impl is checked later
quiz.q: How do dyn Trait and impl Trait differ?

takeaway: dyn for heterogeneity, impl for static speed.
trap: dyn without Box/& unsized error; trait objects need indirection.

body_md: Object safety: traits with generics or `Self` returns cannot be `dyn`. Workarounds: `enum_dispatch`, static impl, or split trait. Compiler error tells which method breaks it.
code:
trait T { fn f(&self); } // object-safe
// trait Bad { fn f<T>(x: T); } // not object-safe
hook: This trait can never be dyn — the compiler knows why.
output: // compiles: T is object-safe; generic Bad can never be dyn

quiz.explain: A vtable needs one entry per method; a generic method would need infinitely many, and returning Self needs a known size.
options: Any trait at all, as long as it is in scope
Only traits whose methods are all async fn
Only marker traits that declare no methods at all
Ones with no generic or Self-returning methods
quiz.q: Which traits can be used as dyn Trait?

takeaway: Keep dyn traits generic-free and Self-free.
trap: Adding generic helper to dyn trait breaks all dyn users.

body_md: **GATs** (generic associated types) allow `type Gat<'a>` in traits — lending iterators, async traits. Stabilized in 1.65. Enables `trait Lending { type Item<'a>; }`.
code: trait Lend { type Out<'a> where Self: 'a; fn get(&self) -> Self::Out<'_>; }
hook: Traits with lifetimes inside types — GATs unlocked them.

quiz.explain: GATs let an associated type take parameters, e.g. type Item<'a>, so a lending iterator can yield items that borrow from itself.
options: Associated types with their own parameters
Associated consts evaluated at compile time
Trait methods that dispatch without a vtable
Default method bodies generated by macros
quiz.q: What do GATs (generic associated types) enable?

takeaway: GATs express lending abstractions in traits.
trap: Overusing GATs where simple assoc type suffices complicates bounds.

body_md: **Const generics** `<const N: usize>` parameterize by values: `struct Arr<T, const N: usize>([T; N])`. No more macro hacks for fixed sizes. Bounds improving each release.
hook: Generics over numbers, not just types — arrays finally generic.

quiz.explain: Const generics take values, not types: B<4> and B<8> are distinct types, so arrays like [T; N] can be generic over length.
options: A lifetime named N tied to the struct
A type parameter N bounded by usize
A trait bound N that usize implements
A compile-time value N of type usize
quiz.q: What does struct B<const N: usize> parameterize?

takeaway: Const generics encode sizes in the type system.
trap: Complex const exprs still unstable; keep bounds simple.

body_md: **Type-state** encodes state in types: `Conn<Disconnected>` vs `Conn<Connected>`. Methods only exist on valid state. Illegal flows fail to compile — zero runtime checks.
hook: Type-state: make illegal protocol states fail to compile.
output: // compiles: connect() moves C<Off> → C<On>; Off has no other methods

quiz.explain: send() exists only on Conn<Connected>, so calling it on Conn<Disconnected> fails to compile. Enums and bools only check at runtime.
options: An enum state field matched at runtime
Type-state: Conn<Connected> has send()
A connected: bool checked inside send()
A debug_assert! at the top of send()
quiz.q: How do you forbid send-before-connect at compile time?

trap: State explosion for many flags; use bitflags or enums instead.

body_md: `PhantomData<T>` marks unused type params: `struct H<T> { ptr: *mut u8, _m: PhantomData<T> }`. Controls variance, drop-check, Send/Sync inference for FFI handles.
code:
use std::marker::PhantomData;
struct H<T> { p: *mut u8, _m: PhantomData<T> }
hook: PhantomData: a zero-byte field that changes everything.
output: // compiles: PhantomData<T> carries variance + drop-check fiction

quiz.explain: PhantomData<T> is zero-sized but tells the compiler the type acts as if it owns a T, which drives variance, drop check, and Send/Sync.
options: Reserving heap space for a T allocated later
Inserting a memory fence for T accesses
Acting as if it owns T, with zero size
Storing T inline without running its Drop

takeaway: PhantomData tunes variance and ownership fiction.
trap: Wrong Phantom (T vs &T) changes variance and breaks Send.

body_md: **Zero-cost** means abstractions compile to hand-written assembly: iterators, impl Trait, Cow fast path. Verify with `cargo asm` or godbolt — trust but check codegen.
hook: Zero-cost abstractions: high-level code, hand-written speed.

quiz.explain: Iterator adapters are generic and monomorphized, so LLVM inlines them into a plain loop. Rust has no JIT, GC, or reflection.
options: They inline down to the same loop you'd write
They are lazily boxed and cached at runtime
The runtime JIT optimizes them after warm-up runs
They use reflection to skip bounds checks
quiz.q: Why are Rust iterator chains zero-cost?

trap: dyn in hot loop adds vtable cost; prefer impl Trait there.

body_md: Newtype plus `From`/`Deref` builds safe wrappers: `struct Meters(f64)`. No mixing units. `impl From<f64> for Meters` enables `.into()` conversions.
hook: Stop mixing meters and feet — newtypes make it impossible.

quiz.explain: A type alias is just another name for f64, so mixing compiles. A newtype is a distinct type, so passing f64 as Meters fails.
options: type Meters = f64; as a type alias
A newtype such as struct Meters(f64)
A Meters trait implemented for f64
A doc comment marking the f64 as meters
quiz.q: How do you keep Meters from mixing with plain f64?

takeaway: Newtypes add domain safety for free.
trap: type Meters = f64 alias gives zero protection; use struct.

body_md: Marker traits `Send/Sync/Copy` carry no methods — only promises. `PhantomData`, auto-traits, and negative impls (`!Send`) tune them. Respect auto-trait leakage.
code:
struct NoSend(*mut u8); // !Send auto
fn main() {}
hook: Marker traits: zero methods, yet they control everything.

quiz.explain: Raw pointers are !Send and !Sync, and auto traits propagate, so the struct loses both unless you add an unsafe impl.
options: Nothing; Send and Sync ignore raw pointers
It makes the struct Send but not Sync
It makes the struct neither Send nor Sync
It makes the struct Sync but not Send
quiz.q: What does a raw *mut T field do to a struct?

takeaway: Markers encode safety promises in types.
trap: Adding unsafe Send to racing type is UB.

body_md: Higher-ranked bounds `for<'a> Fn(&'a str)` accept any lifetime. Needed for callbacks over borrowed data. Appears in `Fn` trait sugar and trait objects.
hook: For any lifetime whatsoever — HRTB is the universal quantifier.
output: // compiles: call accepts any for<'a> Fn(&'a str)

quiz.explain: for<'a> is universal quantification: F must work for any lifetime the caller picks, which callbacks over borrowed data need.
options: The bound picks one fixed lifetime 'a
'a must be 'static for the bound to hold
'a defaults to the enclosing fn's lifetime
The bound must hold for every possible 'a
quiz.q: What does for<'a> mean in a trait bound?

trap: Missing for<'a> ties callback to one short lifetime.

body_md: Trait coherence: one impl per (Trait, Type) globally. Newtype pattern wraps foreign types to impl foreign traits. Keeps ecosystem conflict-free.
hook: Why you cannot just impl Display for Vec — coherence.
output: // compiles: newtype W may impl foreign Display

quiz.explain: The orphan rule requires the trait or the type to be local. A local newtype wrapper makes the type yours, so the impl is allowed.
options: Wrap the type in a local newtype first
Add #[allow(orphan)] above the impl
Put the impl in a module named after it
Transmute it to a local type at call sites
quiz.q: How do you impl a foreign trait for a foreign type?

takeaway: Newtype to satisfy orphan rule cleanly.

body_md: `impl Trait` + `dyn` combine: `fn f() -> impl Into<Box<dyn E>>` hides builder while allowing heterogeneity. Static at edge, dynamic inside — best of both.
hook: Static outside, dynamic inside — combine both dispatch modes.
output:
error[E0277]: the trait bound `Box<dyn E>: From<Box<S>>` is not satisfied
// fix: `Box::new(S) as Box<dyn E>`

quiz.explain: impl Trait hides the concrete type and stays statically dispatched at the boundary, while Box<dyn> erases varied types inside.
options: Return dyn everywhere, even at the API edge
impl Trait at the edge, Box<dyn> inside
Make every function generic over a T
Return the concrete builder type directly
quiz.q: How do you hide a builder yet allow mixed types?

takeaway: Hybrid dispatch balances speed and flexibility.
trap: Nesting dyn in hot path without measuring vtable cost.
